example.answer: The hypotenuse is 10, the adjacent side is about 8.66, and the other angle is 60°.
example.problem: In a right triangle, one acute angle is 30° and the side opposite it is 5. Find the other sides and the other angle.
steps: The hypotenuse comes from sine: sin(30°) = opposite ÷ hypotenuse, so hypotenuse = 5 ÷ sin(30°) = 5 ÷ 0.5 = 10.
The adjacent side comes from tangent: tan(30°) = opposite ÷ adjacent, so adjacent = 5 ÷ tan(30°) = 5 ÷ 0.5774 ≈ 8.66.
example.title: A 30° angle with opposite side 5

faqs.a: The one across from the angle you are interested in. In a right triangle there are two acute angles, and 'opposite' and 'adjacent' are always named relative to the angle you picked — swap the angle and the labels swap too.
faqs.q: Which side is the opposite side?

faqs.a: SOH-CAH-TOA: Sine = Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent ÷ Hypotenuse, Tangent = Opposite ÷ Adjacent. Pick the line that contains the two sides you know (or the one you want) plus the angle.
faqs.q: How do I remember which ratio to use?

faqs.a: It cannot — the hypotenuse is always the longest side, so a leg can never exceed it. If your numbers say otherwise, the opposite and hypotenuse labels are swapped, or the triangle is not right-angled.
faqs.q: Can the opposite side be longer than the hypotenuse?

faqs.a: Yes, and it is often the faster route. Once you know one acute angle in a right triangle, the other is 90° minus it, because the three angles must add to 180° and the right angle already takes 90°.
faqs.q: Do I need trigonometry to find the second angle?

formula.label: Sine (SOH)
formula.note: Use when the opposite side or hypotenuse is involved.

formula.label: Cosine (CAH)
formula.note: Use when the adjacent side or hypotenuse is involved.

formula.label: Tangent (TOA)
formula.note: Use when both legs are involved.

formula.label: Inverse: angle from two sides
formula.note: arcsin and arccos work the same way with the hypotenuse.

howItWorks: Every right triangle is a scaled copy of a triangle fixed by its angles, so the ratios of its sides depend only on the angle, not on the size. Sine, cosine and tangent are just names for three of those ratios: sine is opposite over hypotenuse, cosine is adjacent over hypotenuse, and tangent is opposite over adjacent. SOH-CAH-TOA is the standard memory aid.

If you know an acute angle and one side, the calculator picks the ratio that links the known side to the side you want, then rearranges it. Knowing the opposite side and the angle, the hypotenuse is opposite ÷ sin(angle). Each missing side comes out of the ratio that fits, and the second acute angle is always 90° minus the first.

If you know two sides instead, the calculator runs the ratios backwards with an inverse function: opposite and adjacent give arctan, opposite and hypotenuse give arcsin, adjacent and hypotenuse give arccos. Before it trusts the answer it checks that a leg is never longer than the hypotenuse, which would be impossible in a right triangle.
intro: Solve any right triangle: give one acute angle plus one side to find the other two sides, or give any two sides to find the acute angle. Every step uses SOH-CAH-TOA so you can see exactly which ratio did the work.

mistakes.text: Opposite and adjacent are named relative to the angle you chose. If you switch to the other acute angle, the side you called opposite becomes the adjacent side. Label the sides for one angle and stick with it.
mistakes.title: Mixing up opposite and adjacent

mistakes.text: Trigonometry on this page uses degrees. An angle of 0.5 on a calculator in radian mode is about 28.6°, not half a degree — make sure your calculator and this page agree on degrees.
mistakes.title: Using radians instead of degrees

mistakes.text: The hypotenuse must be the longest side. If the side you called the hypotenuse is shorter than a leg, the labels are wrong or the triangle is not right-angled, and arcsin or arccos would fail.
mistakes.title: Calling the wrong side the hypotenuse

mistakes.text: Rounding the hypotenuse to 2 decimals and then using it to find a leg compounds the error. The calculator keeps full precision internally and rounds only the displayed answer — do the same on paper.
mistakes.title: Rounding between steps
